generatedProse.concept-context: A sport therapy exam often asks you to assess an injury scenario or justify a rehabilitation plan under time pressure, so exam-day strategy decides how much of your revision reaches the page. Arriving settled and reading the whole paper first stop you writing everything you know about a joint instead of answering the question asked. Dividing time by the marks, and planning a brief line of clinical reasoning before writing, protect the applied, evaluative answers the subject rewards.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport therapy and rehabilitation students, equally well revised, sit the same two-hour exam with two case questions.

Tom arrives just in time and hurries to his desk, flustered. With one pen and no watch, he scans the paper, recognises the word ankle in the first case, and writes everything he knows about ankle injuries. That answer runs well over an hour, so the second case, on shoulder rehabilitation, is rushed and half planned. His knowledge was there; his strategy let it leak away.

Amara arrives early, lays out her pens and a watch, and reads both cases before choosing. Seeing they carry equal marks, she gives each an hour, spends ten minutes planning her assessment and rehab reasoning, and writes to that plan. When time runs short on the second case, she closes it with a brief management summary rather than leaving it unfinished. Her preparation showed because her time was controlled.

Both knew the material. Only Amara protected that knowledge with timing and a calm start, and so turned it into a complete paper.
generatedProse.summary: Exam-day strategy is how prepared knowledge in the School of Sport becomes marks. You can now explain how an organised approach manages anxiety and protects performance, analyse contrasting approaches to spot the decisions that matter, and devise a timed plan for an exam of your own. With active revision behind you and a clear plan for the day, your preparation has the best chance to show.

check.body: In the worked example, which decision most clearly cost Tom marks?

items.text: Spending well over an hour on the first case, which left the second rushed.
Arriving a few minutes before the start.
Recognising the word ankle in the first case.
Bringing only one pen to the exam.

feedback.correct: That's right. Letting the first case run well over an hour left too little time for the second.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the decision about how Tom spent his time across the two cases.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The clearest cost was spending well over an hour on the first case, which left the second rushed. The late arrival and single pen added stress but did not directly lose the marks.
